content.p: On the night of 24 May 1856, a small party of armed men went from cabin to cabin along Pottawatomie Creek in eastern Kansas Territory and took five pro-slavery settlers out into the dark. By the next morning all five were dead. The killings near Dutch Henry's Crossing became known as the Pottawatomie massacre, and the man most often named as its leader was John Brown, an anti-slavery activist who had come to Kansas the year before. The Kansas Historical Society links the night to the guerrilla fighting that the press had begun to call "Bleeding Kansas" that spring. Who gave the orders, how many men took part, and what happened in the last minutes of each victim's life are questions the surviving accounts answer in different ways.

Kansas Territory was organized by Congress in 1854, and the question of whether slavery would be allowed was left to the settlers. Slaveholders from neighboring Missouri moved in, but they were outnumbered by farmers from Kentucky, Tennessee and elsewhere who owned no slaves and had no wish to see slavery spread. Rival elections produced two territorial governments, and each side regarded the other as illegitimate. By 1856 the territory had become a place of raids and reprisals on both sides.

Brown had grown up in a devoutly religious family in Ohio. According to History Today, he believed that the return of Christ was being held back by slavery. He had married twice and fathered many children, and his business ventures had mostly failed. In 1855 several of his grown sons moved to the new territory and asked him for weapons to defend themselves against men from Missouri. Brown went to them that September with a wagon loaded with swords, guns and gunpowder, and he settled at Osawatomie, where he was given command of an anti-slavery militia company. The Kansas Historical Society describes him as using religious and moral reasons to justify what he later did.
content.h2: Lawrence and the Attack on Sumner
content.p: In May 1856 a force of pro-slavery men, supported by the local sheriff, attacked the anti-slavery town of Lawrence. The Free State Hotel, the office of a Lawrence newspaper and other property were destroyed. The Kansas Historical Society says the Pottawatomie killings came a few days after that raid.

News from Washington reached Kansas at about the same time. Senator Charles Sumner had demanded that Kansas be admitted to the Union as a free state, and two days later South Carolina Congressman Preston Brooks beat him with a cane on the Senate floor, leaving him bleeding and unconscious. History Today reports that supporters of Brooks in the South sent him replacement canes. Witnesses said Brown was enraged when he heard of the attack on Sumner. Brown told his company that he intended to take "a radical retaliatory measure" that would involve "some killing." History Today describes his target as the "slave hounds" at the small settlement on Pottawatomie Creek.
content.h2: The Night at Dutch Henry's Crossing
content.p: Several accounts, including a statement made in 1879 by James Towsley, a member of the party who later became a witness, agree on the basic sequence. Towsley's account, as reprinted by the Olathe district schools' local history guide, says the party left a Free State camp on the afternoon of 23 May and camped about a mile above Dutch Henry's Crossing. After supper, Brown told the men what he intended: to "sweep the Pottawatomie of all pro-slavery men living on it." Towsley says he refused to guide them to the settlements and that Brown put the expedition off by a day. The Legends of America page, which reprints the 1912 state cyclopedia, says Brown first meant to take the men prisoner and hold a trial, and that his plan changed after Doyle tried to escape.

The party went first to the cabin of James P. Doyle, north of the creek. Brown and some of his sons went to the door, and Doyle and his sons William and Drury were taken into the road. According to Towsley, Doyle was shot in the forehead and the two younger men were cut down with swords. The party then went to the house of Allen Wilkinson, who was taken out and killed in the road a short distance from his door.

The party then crossed Pottawatomie Creek and reached the home of the Sherman brothers, known locally as Dutch Henry, Dutch Bill and Dutch Pete. Dutch Henry was not at home, and the men there were questioned. William Sherman was taken to the creek and killed. The Kansas Historical Society's account says five men were killed, and the state's 1912 cyclopedia gives the same total. Mrs. Wilkinson's letter, printed in an Illinois newspaper and reprinted in a historical journal, describes her husband being taken away by men she did not know.

The five dead men were all pro-slavery in their politics, although that label covered very different lives. Allen Wilkinson was the most prominent of the five. He ran the post office for the settlers along the creek, sat in the territorial legislature, and served part time in the territory's courts. James Doyle had taken up a claim north of the creek in the fall of 1854, and his sons William, aged 22, and Drury, aged 20, lived with him. William Sherman was one of the brothers who had settled on an abandoned Indian farm at the ford that became known as Dutch Henry's Crossing.

Some Free State men did not regard the victims as harmless. The 1912 cyclopedia states that Wilkinson had been elected to the legislature by fraud and violence and had voted for a "black code," that the Doyle sons kept Free State men from the polls by force, and that the Shermans gave shelter to lawless invaders. The cyclopedia adds that not everyone shared this view. Johannsen's 1956 footnote, published by the Kansas Historical Society, says the men were summoned from their cabins and found the next day where they had fallen.

Wilkinson's family suffered afterward. A letter written at the request of Mrs. Wilkinson, and printed by the Alton Weekly Courier in Illinois, describes four men she did not know asking her husband to surrender, taking him away, and leaving her, sick with measles, behind. Her brother-in-law, Henry James, later wrote to Senator Stephen A. Douglas. He asked for a land grant for the widow and children, because the claim Wilkinson had sold him that April was lost after the killings.

Most accounts name John Brown as the leader, but they differ on the rest of the party. The Kansas Historical Society says it is generally believed that Brown led four of his sons and three other men. History Today gives four sons and two or three others. Malin's 1940 article, based on the testimony taken by a congressional minority member, lists four sons, a son-in-law and two other settlers. Towsley's 1879 statement names Brown, four sons (Frederick, Oliver, Owen and Watson), a son-in-law named Henry Thompson, a man named Weiner and himself, with Frederick Brown posted to guard the road. The count therefore runs from seven to eight men, depending on the account.

Towsley's statement is a detailed eyewitness narrative, but it was given 23 years after the events, and the Republican Citizen of Paola printed it in the middle of a newspaper dispute. The Paola paper's introduction says that James Redpath and other Eastern abolitionists had argued that Brown was not present when the murders were committed. The paper's headline states flatly that Brown was the leader. Towsley's account is therefore a participant's account with an obvious interest, and the Kansas Historical Society's wording reflects that uncertainty.
content.h2: The Congressional Committee and the Harris Affidavit
content.p: A special House committee was investigating the Kansas troubles when the killings happened. Malin's 1940 article identifies its members as John Sherman of Ohio, William A. Howard of Michigan and Mordecai Oliver of Missouri. The two anti-slavery members took the view that the killings had occurred after the committee was appointed and so lay outside its scope. Oliver, a pro-slavery Democrat, disagreed. Malin says Oliver took affidavits from Mrs. Doyle, her surviving young son, Mrs. Wilkinson and James Harris, and printed them with his minority report.

Harris's affidavit is the central witness statement about the night's events at the Sherman house. Harris said three men were staying with him: William Sherman, a man named John S. Whiteman and a stranger. Brown's men took each of them out separately and questioned them. The stranger and Harris were allowed to return to the house, while William Sherman did not come back. His body was found the next morning on the edge of the creek. Malin describes the wound on the head and states that Free State men later argued that Harris had been pressured into signing. Malin notes that Harris had also sworn, in a claim for losses filed in 1857, that Brown had stolen a horse, saddle, bridle and gun on the night of the killing and that threats had forced him to leave his property. A neighbor and another witness supported Harris's account of his fear. Malin notes that little interest has been shown in who the stranger was.

The stranger's identity is itself disputed. Christian, a lawyer, gave an account in which a traveler named Jerome Glanville had been kept prisoner at Dutch Henry's until morning and then released. Harris's version says the stranger had bought a cow and was allowed to stay in the house. Malin says Christian's story of blood-stained hands "scarcely rings true."

The Kansas Historical Society reports that the killings were denounced by Southern newspapers and by some in the North. Governor Shannon, who had struggled to bring order to the territory, resigned in August 1856. Brown fought at Black Jack on 2 June 1856, and in August he led free-state men in defending Osawatomie against a pro-slavery attack. History Today gives a different emphasis: it says that after the killings hundreds of armed men gathered on both sides, that pro-slavery men destroyed some of the Brown homesteads, and that Osawatomie was burned at the end of August in revenge for the killings. By the end of the year, History Today says, roughly 200 people had died in the guerrilla fighting.

The killers were never prosecuted, according to History Today. In 1859 Brown raided the United States armory at Harper's Ferry, Virginia. He was captured, tried for treason, conspiracy and murder, and hanged. History Today says abolitionists in the North considered him a saint and martyr.
content.h2: Disputed Accounts and the John Brown Legend
content.p: Malin wrote that as the "John Brown Legend" grew, Free State men tried hard to discredit Harris's story, arguing that undue influence had been used to obtain his affidavit. Malin says the charge should not be taken too seriously, because Harris and others left further affidavits of the same tenor. Malin's point is that little attention has been paid to who the stranger was.

The Olathe reprint of the 1879 Paola article shows how the question was argued in Kansas in the late nineteenth century. Its introduction says that the Lawrence Journal sent John Hutchings to find an eyewitness, and that Hutchings found Towsley. Towsley's statement was used to answer the claim that Brown had not been present. Whether it settles the matter depends on whether one accepts a participant's own statement given long after the event. The Kansas Historical Society's wording stops short of that. It says Brown is generally believed to have led the killings, and it presents the attribution as a belief, not a finding.

The record is therefore uneven. The names of the victims, the date and the place are consistently reported. The size of Brown's party, the sequence of the killings, the fate of William Sherman and the reasons for the night's plan are not. Readers who want more detail should consult Malin's full 1940 article, which discusses the affidavits taken for the congressional minority.
